1:
Ellicott sets the stakes: as with Ishmael and Isaac, an election had to be declared, but where Abraham obeyed with a heavy heart, Isaac struggled against God's will and had his assent extracted by craft. He contrasts the brothers — Esau vigorous but caring for nothing beyond earthly things, Jacob sedentary and calculating yet valuing what Esau despised — and blames both sides, the artifices of Rebekah and Jacob no less than Isaac's attempt to annul a plain prophecy. His age they dispute: Gill and Henry put him near a hundred and thirty-five, Gill noting this was Ishmael's age at death; Clarke and Ellicott make him a hundred and seventeen, Clarke naming the higher figure as merely the received opinion and rejecting it. All agree he outlived the scene by forty years, and Ellicott adds that old is so loose a word here that Samuel is called old when at most middle-aged.

Henry allows Isaac the charitable reading, that he was not knowing, or not understanding, or not duly considering the oracle, and was governed by natural affection more than he should have been — whence he draws that we take our measures from our own reason rather than revelation, expecting the promise to fall to the mighty and noble, though God does not see as man sees; Wesley repeats him almost verbatim. Keil and Delitzsch are severe: Isaac held to his preference without regard to the words spoken before the birth and took no notice of Esau's bartered birthright or his Canaanite marriages, and the infirmity of his flesh appears in his wanting his spirits raised by a dish of venison. Calvin raises the transaction instead. The blessing was no mere prayer but a legitimate sanction divinely interposed to make election manifest, so that Isaac stood there as a prophet and interpreter of God rather than as a father; that God let him be deceived proves to Calvin that no human will raised Jacob; and he observes that Isaac's attachment to his son was a blindness hindering him more than the dimness of his eyes.

The hunting gear divides Clarke from Ellicott. Both note that the word occurs nowhere else and comes from a root meaning to hang; Ellicott makes it something like our hanger, a sort of knife, while allowing that the Targum and Syriac read a sword and nothing certain can be said. Clarke would have guessed a shield had the Greek and Latin not made it a quiver, and rejects the hanger comparison outright, since that word entered English only after the Crusades from a Persian name for a dagger. On the meat Clarke argues that the blessing was a divine right requiring ceremony, no covenant being binding unless the parties had eaten together, so Isaac could not convey it until he had eaten what the receiver provided. Ellicott offers a household detail instead: an Arab sheikh's rare dish of flesh is dressed with almonds, pistachios and raisins, so a kid would not easily be told from an antelope.

On Rebekah the three differ in temper. Clarke is hardest: some claim she had a divine intimation, but one so instructed would not have needed deceit, and she took the most exceptionable means available. Ellicott divides the blame — had her faith been pure she would have known God could keep his word without her, yet the fault began with Isaac, and she probably thought she was preventing a grievous wrong. Calvin holds both ends at once. Her stratagem was faulty, and she sinned the more in sporting with wiles in a sacred matter, darkening the oracle she trusted; yet her readiness to provoke her husband, set the brothers at enmity and risk the son she loved could have sprung from nothing but faith — a pure knowledge not always so governing the pious that they never slide while holding the right course.
6:
Henry draws up a balance sheet. The end was good, since Rebekah had the oracle to direct her; the means were bad and no way justifiable. It wronged Isaac, taking advantage of his infirmity, and Jacob, whom she taught to deceive by putting a lie into his mouth, or at least into his right hand; and left him open to scruples afterwards, since the blessing might be revoked as given by mistake of the person. Henry sets out the honest course instead — a humble reminder of the oracle, and a showing that Esau had forfeited it by selling the birthright and marrying strange wives — and thinks Isaac would probably have been prevailed on to bless Jacob knowingly; God left her to herself that he might have the glory of bringing good out of evil. Wesley reproduces the argument closely. Ellicott notes that her report adds the covenant name and defends her against the charge of inventing it, since only the main sense of Isaac's words is recorded; the phrase meant more to Jacob than to Esau, who valued the blessing chiefly for its temporal good.

Jacob's hesitation is read three ways. Calvin calls it very contrary to faith, a man who debates with himself showing himself deficient, and adds a second error, that he dreaded his father's anger rather than reverencing God, a right end not making an oblique course lawful. Yet he will not leave it there: faith prevailed, for why else prefer a bare and seemingly empty benediction to the quiet he enjoyed and to life itself? Even the fear of his father sprang from the true fear of God, since no one would so dread a verbal censure who did not reckon the grace in his father's hands worth more than a thousand lives. Clarke is sharper: the law against making the blind wander was understood even then, and Jacob seems at this moment to have had a more tender conscience than his mother.

Over Rebekah's answer they part again. Gill reports the Targum's turn, that she had been told in prophecy no curse would fall on her son, and reads her words as strong faith in the oracle. Clarke calls that paraphrase curious and the undertaking a dreadful responsibility, and lays down the principle that the sacred writer states facts as they were but nowhere says any man should copy them, often relating what he never recommends. Ellicott observes that no curse followed, Isaac afterwards owning the substantial justice of the act and confirming the blessing, yet finds it strange that neither scrupled at the immorality, apparently thinking a right end justified falsehood. Calvin says she sins again, burning with a zeal so hasty that she never asks how God regards it and, having no command, takes her own counsel; but he grants the zeal sprang from reverence for God's word. His strongest argument is from Balaam: if a venal tongue could be forced to bless the elect people against its owner's wish, how much more easily the tongue of Isaac, who wished to obey and erred only in his affection.

The disguise draws out the details. Clarke reports Ainsworth's argument that the goodly raiment was a set of holy robes, the priest under the law having garments to minister in, and asks why else Esau's own wives did not keep them rather than his mother, who stored them against moths. Ellicott agrees, supposing the elder son held a priestly office and ministered for his failing father, since ordinary raiment would not have been kept in the mother's tent. On the skins he cautions that oriental goats are famous for soft silky wool whereas hair on a man's body is never delicate — which is why Henry says Esau must have been rough indeed if nothing less would serve. Henry adds that Providence has so ordered features that no two faces are alike.
18:
Henry marvels that so plain a man could play the part, and concludes that lying is soon learnt. He counts the untruths: that he was Esau, that he had done as his father bade him when he had no command, that the dish was venison when it came from the fold — and worst, that he fathered it on God. It is written, Henry says, not for imitation but for admonition, good men having failed in the very graces for which they were most eminent. Gill draws a finer line: claiming only the birthright he might have been excused, having bought it, but saying he was Esau admits no defence. Clarke will allow no palliation, reporting Calmet's division of the fraud into words, actions and clothing, and objecting that men have laboured not merely to excuse the pair but to show the thing was according to the mind of God. Calvin marks the change of nerve: timid at first, Jacob now lies confidently, which teaches that a man once past the bounds of duty soon allows himself unmeasured license.

Isaac's suspicion is roused and then quieted. Ellicott finds two things that woke it: the game came back too quickly, having to be sought far from the pastures, and the answer about providence was not Esau's way of thinking, so Jacob broke character. He adds that the twins' voices had their peculiarities and Isaac caught the difference, but the kid-skins fitted cleverly and the doubt vanished at a touch. Keil and Delitzsch note the direct question was put to dispel the suspicion the voice had raised. Clarke puts the failure down to illness, since a man who cannot tell a kid's hide from his son's arm has a sense of feeling much impaired. Henry turns the moment into a figure: the voice was Jacob's and the hands Esau's, the very picture of a hypocrite who speaks like a saint and works like a sinner — and the judgment, as here, goes by the hands. Calvin faces the awkwardness that the blessing seems void for want of faith in the man who gave it, and answers that God worked by Isaac's hand without making the instrument a willing party, as pastors reconcile men to God by his command yet cannot discern where their seed will bear.

The scent settles it. Clarke supposes aromatic herbs laid up with the garments, a custom still kept where thyme and lavender are put in wardrobes, sprigs laid in eastern manuscripts against worms, and Russia leather carried among clothes to the Indies. Ellicott notes that the pastures of Palestine are fragrant, and suspects Isaac meant to contrast a life in the open field with the odour of the cattle-shed, not knowing which son stood before him. Calvin is content with Ambrose's allegory, that the younger is blessed under the person of the elder in borrowed garments whose odour pleases the father, as we are blessed entering God's presence in Christ's name.

Henry sorts what was given under three heads: plenty, with heaven and earth concurring; power over his brethren; and a standing with God, whose friendship and enmity should follow his own. More is comprised in it than appears, entailing the promise of the Messiah and of the church. Wesley follows him throughout. Ellicott observes that the divine name shifts, the God of nature being properly invoked for dew and fat places, and notes where Isaac stops — he gives the birthright and its precedence but not the promise that in him all families should be blessed, for which he offers three reasons: that such a gift is God's, not man's; that he doubted Esau's worthiness; or that his own wrong conduct narrowed his sight. Clarke, after Bishop Newton, divides it differently: in temporal advantages the brothers were to be much alike, but the promise of the blessed seed could be given to one only.
30:
Isaac's trembling is read four ways. Clarke prefers the marginal rendering, that he trembled with a great trembling greatly, and takes it for the concern of a man who sees how he has been deceived. Gill lists four causes — Jacob's craft, Esau's loss, his own act against his own intention, and an overruling providence fulfilling the oracle exactly, which he thinks may only now have come fresh into Isaac's mind. Ellicott denies it was vexation: Isaac felt he had been resisting God, and the proof is that he persists no longer, has no word of blame for Rebekah or Jacob, and confirms the blessing outright. Calvin says the faith long smothered in him shines out and emits fresh sparks, since the fear itself sprang from faith. Wesley adds that men who follow their affections rather than the divine will involve themselves in such perplexities, and supposes Isaac either recollected the oracle or felt himself unusually filled with the Spirit, so that he perceived God saying Amen to it.

Esau's cry Henry calls a great and bitter one that made his father's tent ring, noting that the man who made light of the birthright now found no place of repentance. Calvin will not soften it: the tears are desperation rather than piety, and Esau enters by no gate of faith, asking a second blessing as though his father could breathe them out indiscriminately when only one had been deposited with him. Worse, he shows no penitence, accusing his brother and taking no blame himself, though repentance begins in grief for one's own sin. On the word Isaac used, Gill notes that the Targums and Jarchi soften it to wisdom, but insists it means fraud, and suspects Isaac said it partly to clear himself with Esau. Clarke lets Esau call the old sale a robbery, Jacob having taken advantage of a perishing man. Ellicott observes that Esau's play on his brother's name has been a lasting revenge, the bad sense he first put on it sticking ever since, though the word properly means one who follows close on another's heels.

Calvin then makes the comparison that most unsettles the scene. Set their works side by side and Esau shows the better: he obeys his father, brings the produce of his own hunting, prepares the food by his own labour, and speaks nothing but truth — whence Calvin concludes that what Jacob obtained was a free gift and nothing earned. He adds that Esau, hearing nothing was left, took courage in the wrong direction, turning to the flesh when he should have drawn from the one fountain and submitted to his brother rather than cut himself off. Ellicott puts the limit plainly: only one son could inherit the spiritual prerogative and the lordship with it, so Esau must be content with some mitigation.

What that mitigation was is itself disputed. Ellicott reports that most modern expositors take the preposition the other way, so that Esau's dwelling shall be away from and not of the fat places of the earth, and calls the familiar rendering of the last clause scarcely more than a guess by two or three old Jewish commentators, the word meaning to toss the yoke — which he traces through Edom's history, long a dependency of Judah, revolting under Joram and again under Ahaz, and reconquered by Hyrcanus. Wesley reads the grant as real but inferior, dew standing first in Jacob's blessing and fatness first in Esau's, according to what each valued most, and Esau gaining some power but never dominion over his brother. Clarke, again with Bishop Newton, takes the sword to mean not perpetual war but a fierce temper living by hunting and raid. Calvin observes that none of it was fulfilled in Esau himself, Jacob having tendered him obedience on the way home, so that the prophecy looked past both men to their posterity.
41:
Henry puts Esau in the way of Cain, hating a brother for no reason but that his father blessed him and God loved him, and calls the hatred causeless and cruel, since nothing less than blood would satisfy it; he wonders how a man could say the word brother and vow his death in one breath. Gill notes what Esau grudged: a better country, greater plenty and dominion, the promise of the Messiah being no concern of his. Calvin makes the threat worse than murder, since Esau knew his father was the herald of the benediction and now prepares to abolish a decree of God with the sword. Both Clarke and Ellicott explain the timing by the funeral, at which the sons were always present, Clarke recalling that Ishmael came from his own country to bury Abraham while in the event both brothers buried Isaac, the enmity long dead. Ellicott reports a proposed rendering that would put the murder before the mourning, and rejects it, since the Hebrew gives it no support and it makes utterly inhuman a man who, with all his faults, had a warm heart.

How Rebekah learned of it Gill leaves open between the rabbis, who make it a revelation, and Aben Ezra, who supposes one of Esau's confidants told her — not at all unlikely, since the man made no secret of it. Keil and Delitzsch gloss Esau's comforting himself as procuring comfort by retaliation. Clarke reports Houbigant's smoother rendering, that Esau was meditating the murder, doubts it is the sense of the original, and is sure he found real pleasure in the prospect. Ellicott adds a second motive: Jacob was now acknowledged heir of the promises and had to marry among his kindred — so that the long journey and the parting came as the immediate fruit of the scheming. Calvin turns the sharpest edge on Rebekah, who by her own deed had put her son in danger of death: mere partiality would have restored the birthright to Esau and removed the cause of quarrel, so her refusal proves extraordinary faith.

The few days she promised are variously reckoned. Gill reports Aben Ezra for a few years and another for one, and observes that Jacob stayed twenty, his mother probably dying first, after which she is never mentioned again. Clarke and Ellicott make the absence forty, Clarke citing the rabbis that she died first, Ellicott adding that Isaac lived to see the return though Rebekah did not. Calvin notes only that the shortness of a suffering supports us under it, and that the Hebrew is literally one days, which no English will render.

On being deprived of both in one day they agree closely. Clarke explains that the avenger of blood, being next of kin, would have killed Esau, so both deaths might fall on one day; Wesley has the murderer sacrificed to justice by magistrate or by God's own hand; Calvin, denying that so mild a man as Jacob endangered his brother, concludes that Rebekah looked for God to avenge the murder and would have been bereaved either way, forced to dread whichever son survived. Clarke turns it into a warning that those who sanctify means by the end compass themselves with their own sparks and lie down in sorrow. Of the excuse to Isaac, Gill says she withheld the threat lest it bring his grey hairs with sorrow to the grave; Clarke says she frames a reason and conceals the true one, doubting whether the fear was real; Calvin acquits her of falsehood, since she neither told the whole truth nor left the whole unsaid, and had cause to spare her husband and not inflame Esau. Wesley alone will not have it: more artifice still, guile once used being used again — for though a blessing came to Jacob's posterity by his lying, it brought him heavy affliction for many years.
